summary: Recommends how popular print job submission protocols should map onto the objects and attributes of the Job Monitoring MIB. This helps different printing systems report job information in a consistent way. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Different printers speak different languages. This is a translation guide so they can all report on a print job in the same words.

questions: how to map job submission protocols to job monitoring mib
how does printing work with snmp
subtitle: Unifying how print job submission protocols report status to monitoring systems.

tldr.problem: Different printing systems use incompatible job submission protocols, making it difficult for monitoring applications to get consistent job status information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends how to map data from 11 popular printing protocols (LPR, IPP, IPDS, PJL, and others) onto the fields of the Job Monitoring MIB, a standard information model for job tracking.
tldr.outcome: Printing systems can now report job status consistently, letting monitoring tools work with any protocol.

facts.label: Protocols covered
facts.value: 11 (LPR/LPD, AppleTalk, IPP, IPDS, DPA, NDPS, PJL, PostScript, PServer, SMB, TIP/SI)

today: RFC 2708 is an Informational memo and remains current as a mapping guide. It was created alongside RFC 2707 (the Job Monitoring MIB itself) in 1999 and continues to be the standard reference for how printing systems should report job information to monitoring applications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Printing systems come in many varieties, each using its own job submission protocol. The Job Monitoring MIB provides a standard way to track print jobs, but different protocols provide their information in different formats. This RFC defines recommended mappings from 11 popular protocols to the Job Monitoring MIB objects and attributes, so monitoring applications can understand job status consistently regardless of which protocol a printer uses.

The mappings are unidirectional: from the job submission protocol to the MIB. The document focuses especially on mapping the jmJobSubmissionID, which lets a client identify a job in the MIB after submitting it. The RFC assumes the Job Monitoring MIB runs either on a printer or on a server, depending on the system configuration.
sections.eli5: Different printers speak different languages. This section explains that we need a translator so monitoring software can understand any printer's job descriptions.

sections.title: Protocols and Mapping Strategies
sections.content:
The RFC covers 11 protocols: LPR/LPD (used by UNIX systems), AppleTalk (Macintosh networks), IPP (Internet Printing Protocol, the most feature-rich), IPDS (Intelligent Printer Data Stream, used with mainframes), DPA (ISO Document Printing Application), NDPS (Novell's protocol, based on DPA), PJL (Printer Job Language by HP), PostScript (via comment strings), NetWare PServer, SMB (Server Message Block, for Windows), and TIP/SI (Transport Independent Printer Interface). Each protocol provides different amounts of job information; richer protocols like IPP provide fields that map directly to MIB objects, while simpler protocols like AppleTalk provide minimal information.

For each protocol, the RFC recommends how to construct the jmJobSubmissionID, a formatted octet string that combines a protocol identifier (a single character like '9' for LPR or '4' for IPP), the host or job owner information, and a job number. When a protocol returns the jmJobIndex directly (as IPP does), the submission ID becomes less necessary.
sections.eli5: There are 11 different printer languages described here. Each one talks about jobs differently, so we explain how to translate each one into the standard language.

sections.title: Job Submission ID and MIB Object Mappings
sections.content:
The jmJobSubmissionID is a 48-octet field: the first octet is a protocol identifier ('9' for LPR/LPD, '4' for IPP, '0' for DPA, 'A' for AppleTalk, 'B' for PServer, 'C' for SMB, 'D' for TIP/SI, 'E' for IPDS/MVS, 'F' for IPDS/VM, 'G' for IPDS/OS400). Octets 2 through 40 hold information about the job origin (hostname, user, queue, or job owner). Octets 41 through 48 contain the job number or jmJobIndex. This format ensures that a monitoring application can look up a job by its submission ID and retrieve the corresponding jmJobIndex from the MIB.

Beyond the submission ID, each protocol maps differently to other MIB objects. IPP is the richest, mapping to job state, state reasons, octets processed, impressions, and many print attributes. LPR/LPD provides minimal mapping: only job owner and the data file size. Simpler protocols like AppleTalk and PostScript have no MIB mappings at all, while PJL and others provide intermediate coverage.
sections.eli5: The job ID is 48 characters long. The first character says which printer language we are using. The middle part says who sent the job. The last part is the job number. That way we can always find the right job in the system.

sections.title: Security and Practical Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the mapping procedures themselves do not introduce new security risks. The mapping happens after the user is already authenticated by the underlying job submission protocol. Because the MIB only stores the job owner's name (not credentials or authorization data), and because there is no "back-door" mechanism to access other security parameters, the mapping preserves the security properties of each protocol.

Practical considerations include the fact that some protocols (like NPrinter/RPrinter, NetWare's lightweight protocol) provide almost no job information at all. For these, implementers are advised to layer a richer protocol such as PJL on top. The RFC also notes that bi-directional protocols like IPP, which return the jmJobIndex directly in the job submission response, reduce or eliminate the need for the jmJobSubmissionID table.
sections.eli5: The mapping does not add new security risks because the printer already checks who the user is before accepting the job. The mapping just translates job descriptions, so private information stays safe.

sections.title: Protocols and Standards Referenced
sections.content:
The RFC references the Job Monitoring MIB itself (RFC 2707), the Line Printer Daemon Protocol (RFC 1179), the Internet Printing Protocol (RFC 2566), the Printer MIB (RFC 1759 for background on MIB conventions), SNMPv2 Textual Conventions (RFC 2579), and numerous external standards including the ISO Document Printing Application (ISO/IEC 10175), the IEEE 1284 standard for parallel port interfaces (TIP/SI), and the IANA registry of character sets.

The document also names the RFC authors and contributors: Ron Bergman (Dataproducts, editor), Tom Hastings (Xerox), Scott Isaacson (Novell), and Harry Lewis (IBM), along with representatives from other manufacturers, all working through the Printer Working Group (PWG).
sections.eli5: This section lists the other standards and documents this RFC is built on, and thanks the people who wrote it.
